messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 62
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Dancer
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 38

He is a 62-year-old Latin American man who has spent most of his adult life in motion, and even now he still thinks of himself first as a dancer. Before the collision, his body feels like an old but trusted instrument: disciplined, expressive, and reliable. He is married, and his home life has a steady rhythm built around work, rehearsals, family routines, and the small rituals he shares with his wife. He describes himself as someone who has always been able to “shake things off” through movement.

That changed the afternoon he was driving home after work and another vehicle struck him at high speed. He remembers the impact as violent and immediate, the world turning into glass, metal, and sound. For a moment he believes he is dying. He cannot get his bearings; his hands feel disconnected from his body, and he is overwhelmed by the smell of airbags, smoke, and blood. He thinks of his wife in a flash and then of his own feet pinned awkwardly in the wreckage. The body he has spent a lifetime training suddenly feels fragile and foreign. In the ambulance he is alternating between panic and numbness, and he keeps asking whether he can still move his legs. Even after he is told he has survived, he cannot fully take in the words.

In the weeks that follow, he returns home physically bruised and shaken, but the more lasting injury is in how he experiences the world. Sleep becomes broken and guarded. He lies awake replaying the crash, hearing again the screech of tires and the crunch of the collision. When he does fall asleep, he is pulled back into it by vivid dreams that leave him sweating and disoriented. During the day, he catches himself scanning intersections, measuring the speed of nearby cars, gripping his seatbelt hard enough to ache. He no longer drives with ease; instead he approaches the car with a tightened chest, as if every trip might become the same catastrophe. He tells himself to stay calm, but his body seems to remember before his mind can reason.

Because he is a dancer, he notices with special distress how the trauma has entered his body. He is hyperaware of aches, stiffness, and any sensation that resembles the moment of impact. Sudden braking on the street makes him flinch. He startles at horns, sirens, and the slam of a door. At rehearsals he is still capable, but he is less free than before. He checks his footing more often, worries about balance, and sometimes feels detached from the music, as if he is watching himself from a distance instead of inhabiting the movement. He keeps going because work matters to him and because dancing is part of who he is, yet there are moments when he steps off the floor feeling drained and secretly frightened that his body is no longer trustworthy.

He becomes more irritable at home, though he does not like this version of himself. His wife notices that he is quieter and more jumpy, and he sometimes snaps when startled or interrupted. He avoids talking about the crash in detail, partly because the memories arrive too vividly when he tries and partly because he does not want to burden his family. At the same time, he is drawn to the memory in a painful way, unable to stop checking news about collisions or watching traffic patterns as if prediction could protect him. He feels ashamed by how much the event still controls his mood and energy. On some days he feels older than his age, slowed by exhaustion and the effort of remaining composed.

Over time, he begins to move through life with a narrower range. He still works, still attends to his marriage, and still dances, but he does so with a sense of vigilance that was not there before. The accident is never far from his mind. Some mornings he wakes already tense, anticipating the day ahead before anything has happened. Yet he also notices that in moments of music or familiar choreography, he can sometimes step back into his body for a few minutes and feel his breath settle. Those moments do not erase what happened, but they remind him that the life he had before the crash is not entirely gone, even if it now exists beside the memory of the wreck.
